Colombia,[d] officially the Republic of Colombia,[e] is a country located in South America, with insular regions in North America. Colombia's mainland is bordered by the Caribbean Sea to the north, Venezuela to the east, Brazil to the southeast, Peru and Ecuador to the south and southwest, the Pacific Ocean to the west, and Panama to the northwest. Colombia is divided into 32 departments. The Capital District of Bogotá is the country's largest city hosting the main financial and cultural hub. Other urban areas include Medellín, Cali, Barranquilla, Cartagena, Bucaramanga, Pereira, Santa Marta, Cúcuta, Ibagué, Villavicencio and Manizales. It covers an area of 1,141,748 square kilometers (440,831 sq mi) and has a population of around 52 million. Its rich cultural heritage[14]—including language, religion, cuisine, and art—reflects its history as a colony, fusing cultural elements brought by immigration from Europe[15][16][17][18] and the Middle East,[19][20][21] with those brought by the African diaspora,[22] as well as with those of Indigenous civilizations that predate colonization.[23] Spanish is the official language, although Creole, English and 64 other languages are recognized regionally.

Colombia has been home to many Indigenous peoples and cultures since at least 12,000 BCE. The Spanish landed in La Guajira in 1499, and by the mid-16th century had colonized much of present-day Colombia, establishing the New Kingdom of Granada. Independence from the Spanish Empire was declared in 1810, with what is now Colombia emerging as the United Provinces of New Granada. After a Spanish reconquest, Colombian independence was secured and the Gran Colombia period began in 1819. The new polity experimented with federalism as the Granadine Confederation (1858) and then the United States of Colombia (1863), before becoming a centralised republic in 1886. With the backing of the US and France, Panama seceded from Colombia in 1903, resulting in Colombia's present borders. Beginning in the 1960s, the country has suffered from an asymmetric low-intensity armed conflict and political violence, both of which escalated in the 1990s. Since 2000, there has been improvement in security, stability, and rule of law, as well as economic growth and development.[24][25]

Colombia is recognized for its healthcare system, being the best healthcare in the Americas according to the World Health Organization and 22nd in the world.[26][27] Its diversified economy is the third-largest in South America, with macroeconomic stability and favorable long-term growth prospects.[28][29] The country has one of the widest recognitions of LGBT rights, gender equality, animal rights, and human rights, permitting same-sex adoption, same-sex marriage, legality of abortion, legality of euthanasia, and animal rights protections.[30][31][32][33][34][35]

Colombia is one of the world's seventeen megadiverse countries; it has the highest level of biodiversity per square mile in the world, and second-highest level overall.[36] Its territory encompasses the Amazon rainforest, highlands, grasslands and deserts. Colombia is a member of global and regional organizations including the UN, the WTO, the OECD, the OAS, the CIVETS, the Pacific Alliance and the Andean Community; it is a NATO Global Partner[37] and a major non-NATO ally of the United States.[38]

Etymology

The name "Colombia" is derived from the last name of the Italian navigator Christopher Columbus (Latin: Christophorus Columbus, Italian: Cristoforo Colombo, Spanish: Cristóbal Colón). It was conceived as a reference to all of the New World.[39] The name was later adopted by the Republic of Colombia of 1819, formed from the territories of the old Viceroyalty of New Granada (modern-day Colombia, Panama, Venezuela, Ecuador, and northwest Brazil).[40]

When Venezuela, Ecuador, and Cundinamarca came to exist as independent states, the former Department of Cundinamarca adopted the name "Republic of New Granada". New Granada officially changed its name in 1858 to the Granadine Confederation. In 1863 the name was again changed, this time to United States of Colombia, before finally adopting its present name – the Republic of Colombia – in 1886.[40]

To refer to this country, the Colombian government uses the terms Colombia and República de Colombia.[41]

Owing to its location, the present territory of Colombia was a corridor of early human civilization from Mesoamerica and the Caribbean to the Andes and Amazon basin. The oldest archaeological finds are from the Pubenza and El Totumo sites in the Magdalena Valley 100 kilometers (62 mi) southwest of Bogotá.[42] These sites date from the Paleoindian period (18,000–8000 BCE). At Puerto Hormiga and other sites, traces from the Archaic Period (~8000–2000 BCE) have been found. Vestiges indicate that there was also early occupation in the regions of El Abra and Tequendama in Cundinamarca. The oldest pottery discovered in the Americas, found in San Jacinto, dates to 5000–4000 BCE.[43][44]

Indigenous people inhabited the territory that is now Colombia by 12,500 BCE. #### Overview

In 2024, global trade of Coffee reached $50.3B, reflecting a 17% increase from 2023, when trade totaled $42.9B. Over the past five years, trade in this category has grown at an annualized rate of 10.9%. 

Among the 1222 products traded in 2024, Coffee ranked 86 in global trade value, accounting for 0.22% of world trade. According to the Product Complexity Index (PCI), it was the 963rd most complex product out of 1056, with a PCI value of -1.41.

#### Exports and Imports

## [Key takeaways about the top 10 coffee exporting countries in 2025]

* Brazil leads all coffee-exporting countries with a record 50.44 million 60-kg bags exported in 2024, up 28.5% year-over-year, with total export value exceeding US$12.5 billion, according to the Coffee Exporters Council (Cecafé).
* Vietnam holds second place with approximately 30 million bags in 2025, the largest Robusta supplier globally, followed by Colombia (12.9 million bags), Indonesia (10.9 million bags), and Ethiopia (8.36 million bags), which together complete the top 5 coffee exporting countries.
* Global coffee production reached approximately 10.5 million metric tons in 2024, up 4% year-over-year, with inventories at their lowest level since 2018 and prices more than doubling due to climate shocks, reshaping trade flows into 2025.

## [Top 10 coffee exporting countries: Which country exports the most coffee in the world?]

Brazil is the world's largest coffee exporter by a wide margin. According to TradeInt trade data, Brazil's coffee exports (HS 0901) reached US$14.92 billion in 2025, a 31.17% increase year-over-year. This is further corroborated by Comunicaffe and the Coffee Exporters Council (Cecafé), which recorded a shipment volume of 50.44 million 60-kg bags in 2024, the highest ever logged by any country. According to the USDA, Brazil and Vietnam together account for 55% of global coffee output, with Brazil alone representing 38%.

Top 10 largest coffee exporting countries by volume in 2024-2025:

1. Brazil - 50.44 million bags (2024 record, +28.5% YoY)

## [How much is Brazil's coffee export worth, and who are its top buyers?]

According to TradeInt trade data, Brazil's coffee exports (HS 0901) totalled US$14.92 billion in 2025, up 31.17% year-over-year. Germany is the single largest buyer, accounting for US$2.30 billion (15.41% of total), followed by the United States at US$1.92 billion (12.85%) and Italy at US$1.33 billion (8.93%). This is consistent with figures from Comunicaffe and the Coffee Exporters Council (Cecafé), which recorded a shipment volume of 50.44 million 60-kg bags in 2024, making Brazil the dominant price-setter for the global Arabica market.

## [Which country is the world's largest Robusta coffee exporter?]

Vietnam is the world's leading supplier of Robusta coffee. According to the USDA Foreign Agricultural Service (FAS) Coffee Annual Report, Vietnam exported approximately 30 million bags in 2025, holding the number-two position globally. TradeInt trade data further reflects the global demand for Robusta, showing that Germany (15.41% share), the United States (12.85%), and Italy (8.93%) are among the top buyers of coffee from major exporting origins in 2025, markets where Vietnamese Robusta underpins a significant share of espresso and commercial blends.
